options.label: Light made by a living thing
options.feedback: A chemical reaction inside the body produces it.

options.label: Light reflected off a shiny body
options.feedback: That is eyeshine or iridescence, not light made.

options.label: Light stored during the day
options.feedback: That is phosphorescence, and living things rarely use it.

options.label: Heat given off as a faint glow
options.feedback: A living body is far too cool to glow with heat.

items.ok_line: Not borrowed, not stored — manufactured on the spot.
items.ko_line: The clue is in the word: bio for life, lumen for light.
items.exp_text: Bioluminescence is light produced by a chemical reaction inside an organism. A molecule called luciferin is oxidised with the help of an enzyme, luciferase, and the energy released comes out as a photon rather than as heat. It has evolved independently more than forty separate times — in bacteria, fungi, insects, molluscs, fish and worms — which is a strong sign of how useful it is.

items.prompt: Why is bioluminescence called cold light?

options.label: Almost none of the energy becomes heat
options.feedback: Nearly all of it leaves as light.

options.label: It only works in cold water
options.feedback: Fireflies glow in warm summer air.

options.label: The animal cools down while glowing
options.feedback: Its temperature does not change.

options.label: The light itself feels cold
options.feedback: Light has no temperature to feel.

items.ok_line: Almost perfect conversion. Nothing is wasted as warmth.
items.ko_line: Cold here describes the process, not the animal or the water.
items.exp_title: Nearly all light, almost no waste
items.exp_text: A firefly converts around 90% of the reaction's energy into light and loses very little as heat, which is why the glow is safe to hold in a closed hand. That is a far better ratio than the glowing filament of an old lamp, which throws away most of its energy as warmth. An animal that produced light by heating something would cook itself.

items.prompt: What two ingredients does most bioluminescence need?

options.label: A fuel and an enzyme to burn it
options.feedback: Luciferin and luciferase, in almost every case.

options.label: A pigment and strong sunlight
options.feedback: Sunlight is not involved at all.

options.label: A mineral and a strong acid
options.feedback: No acid is required.

options.label: Two gases mixed in the blood
options.feedback: Oxygen is used, but the fuel is not a gas.

items.ok_line: A fuel, an enzyme, and oxygen to bring them together.
items.ko_line: One molecule is consumed, another speeds the reaction up. That is the pair.
items.exp_text: The fuel is called luciferin and the enzyme that oxidises it is luciferase — general names, since different groups use chemically different versions. Oxygen is the third requirement, which is why glowing organisms can switch the light off simply by cutting off the oxygen supply. Both names come from the Latin for light-bearer.

items.prompt: Where does most of the world's bioluminescence occur?

options.label: In the deep ocean
options.feedback: Most animals living below the sunlit layer glow.

options.label: In tropical forests
options.feedback: Fireflies and some fungi glow there, but far fewer.

options.label: In caves
options.feedback: A few glow-worms, and little else.

options.label: In freshwater lakes
options.feedback: Bioluminescence is very rare in fresh water.

items.ok_line: The commonest way of making light on Earth is in the dark sea.
items.ko_line: Think of the largest habitat on the planet, and the darkest.
items.exp_title: The dark ocean is full of lamps
items.exp_text: Surveys suggest three quarters of animals in the open ocean below the sunlit zone produce light. Since that habitat is by far the largest on Earth, bioluminescence is the norm for life on this planet and we are the exception. It is almost absent from fresh water, which remains one of the genuinely unexplained facts about it.

items.prompt: Why is nearly all ocean bioluminescence blue?

options.label: Blue travels furthest through water
options.feedback: Water absorbs red within a few metres.

options.label: Blue is the cheapest colour to make
options.feedback: Cost is not what decides the colour.

options.label: Blue frightens predators most
options.feedback: It is the only colour most of them can see.

options.label: Sea water tints the light blue
options.feedback: The light is blue before it leaves the animal.

items.ok_line: The only colour worth making, in a place where red dies in metres.
items.ko_line: Water strips the colours out one by one. Which survives longest?
items.exp_text: Water absorbs long wavelengths fast: red is gone within a few metres, while blue penetrates furthest. So blue-green light is the only kind worth producing at depth, and most deep-sea eyes have narrowed to see nothing else. A few predators have broken the rule — some dragonfish emit red light and can see it, giving them a private beam their prey cannot detect at all.

items.prompt: How does an anglerfish use its light?

options.label: As a lure dangled in front of its mouth
options.feedback: Prey approaches the glow and is taken.

options.label: To see prey in the darkness
options.feedback: A lamp on its own head would blind it.

options.label: To warm the water around it
options.feedback: The light produces essentially no heat.

options.label: To signal to fish of its own kind
options.feedback: The lure is aimed at prey, not at mates.

items.ok_line: Bait on a rod, held just in front of the teeth.
items.ko_line: The light hangs on a stalk in front of its mouth. What is a light in front of a mouth for?
items.exp_title: A fishing rod made of flesh
items.exp_text: The lure is a modified fin spine tipped with a bulb the fish can wave. It does not make the light itself: the bulb houses colonies of bioluminescent bacteria, which the fish feeds and houses in exchange for the glow. Small animals approach the light and are taken. Only the female fishes; the male is a fraction of her size and, in some species, fuses to her body permanently.

items.prompt: How does glowing on its underside help a deep-sea fish hide?

options.label: It cancels its own silhouette
options.feedback: From below it no longer blocks the dim light above.

options.label: It dazzles anything looking up
options.feedback: The glow is faint, matched to the background.

options.label: It makes the fish look larger
options.feedback: The aim is to be seen less, not more.

options.label: It warns predators it is poisonous
options.feedback: Warning signals are bright and obvious.

items.ok_line: It fills in its own shadow, and disappears.
items.ko_line: Looking up from below, a fish is a dark shape against faint light. How would you hide that?
items.exp_text: In the twilight zone a hunter below looks up and sees prey as a dark silhouette against the faint light from above. Many fish and squid counter this by lining their undersides with small light organs and tuning them to match the brightness overhead — some can adjust as the surface light changes with cloud or with depth. The technique is called counter-illumination, and it works so well that navies have studied it.

items.prompt: Why do some sea creatures release a cloud of light when attacked?

options.label: It blinds or distracts the attacker
options.feedback: The animal escapes while the hunter is dealing with it.

options.label: It calls other members of its group
options.feedback: The response is escape, not assembly.

options.label: It heats the water to drive it off
options.feedback: The light produces almost no heat.

options.label: It poisons the water around it
options.feedback: The cloud is light, not toxin.

items.ok_line: The same idea as ink, made of light instead.
items.ko_line: A squid in daylight releases ink. What is the deep-sea equivalent?
items.exp_text: Where ink would be invisible in permanent darkness, several deep-sea squid and shrimp eject a glowing cloud instead, leaving the attacker facing a bright smear while the animal backs into the black. Some worms shed glowing body parts that keep writhing and shining as a decoy. Others do the opposite and use light to summon help — a shrimp's glow can attract a larger predator to attack the one attacking it.

items.prompt: What is the commonest use of light among fireflies?

options.label: Finding and choosing a mate
options.feedback: Each species has its own flash pattern.

options.label: Lighting the ground to feed
options.feedback: The glow is far too weak to light anything.

options.label: Frightening away birds
options.feedback: The signal is aimed at other fireflies.

options.label: Keeping warm on cool nights
options.feedback: The reaction produces almost no heat.

items.ok_line: A signal, with a code that differs from species to species.
items.ko_line: The flashes come in patterns, and each species has its own. What does that suggest?
items.exp_text: Male fireflies fly and flash a pattern specific to their species; females perched below answer with a flash at a precise delay, and the timing is what identifies them to each other. The system is exact enough that a difference of a fraction of a second marks one species from another. Some females of the genus Photuris mimic the answering flash of another species, and eat the male that comes to them.

items.prompt: Why does the glow of many bacteria only start when there are enough of them?

options.label: They sense how many neighbours there are
options.feedback: Chemical signals build up until a threshold is crossed.

options.label: A crowd blocks the light of a single cell
options.feedback: One cell alone genuinely produces nothing.

options.label: They must touch to switch each other on
options.feedback: The signal passes through the water, not by contact.

options.label: Their light needs warmth from the group
options.feedback: The reaction needs no warmth at all.

items.ok_line: They count each other, and switch on together or not at all.
items.ko_line: A single bacterium glowing alone would be invisible. So it waits for what?
items.exp_text: Each cell continually releases a small signal molecule. In open water it drifts away, but in a crowded space the concentration climbs, and above a threshold every cell switches its light genes on at once. The behaviour is called quorum sensing, and it was discovered in a glowing bacterium that lives in the light organ of the bobtail squid. The squid farms them and vents them out each dawn to start again.
